overview: Fundamentally misunderstands human physiology. Blood pH is tightly regulated (7.35–7.45) regardless of diet; if it changed significantly, you would die.
methods: No research. Cites debunked claims and misunderstands how metabolism works. No mention of actual cancer biology. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Nonsense. The body maintains pH through breathing and kidney function, not food. Cancer is caused by genetic mutations, not 'acidic blood'.
source: Wellness Influencer Blog. Author has no medical or scientific credentials. Sells alkaline water machines and supplements.

feedback.summary: This e-book contains no research, rests on a basic misunderstanding of how the body works and comes from an author with no medical or scientific qualifications who sells alkaline water machines. Its only strength is being free to read, which says nothing about whether its claims are true, so it gets the lowest rating.

title.note: Its calm, academic wording presents as fact that diet can change blood pH and so prevent cancer, though the body keeps blood pH steady whatever we eat.

access.note: The e-book is free on the author's website, but being easy to read says nothing about whether its claims are true.

source.note: A wellness blog by an author with no medical or scientific qualifications who sells alkaline water machines and supplements, a clear financial stake in the message (a conflict of interest).

theory.note: It ignores basic physiology (how the body works): blood pH stays between 7.35 and 7.45 whatever you eat; a large change would be fatal.

methods.note: There is no research at all, only debunked claims repeated without data, so there is nothing anyone could check or repeat.

conclusion.note: Blaming cancer on 'acidic blood' ignores that cancer comes from genetic mutations and that breathing and the kidneys, not food, keep blood pH steady.

title: Association between urban green space access and rates of anxiety and depression
overview: Uses satellite imagery to quantify green space and links to mental health survey data. Grounded in environmental psychology and stress-reduction theories.
methods: Cross-sectional study of 15,000 adults across 50 cities. Clever use of objective green space metrics (NDVI from satellites). However, as a correlational study it can't prove causation (maybe wealthier, less stressed people move near parks). Data availability: Summary stats only.
conclusion: Plausible but limited. Shows association but authors acknowledge reverse causation possibility and confounders like income. Calls for experimental interventions.
source: Mid-Tier Environmental Health Journal. Legitimate peer review but not the most rigorous in the field.

feedback.summary: A large, honest study that uses satellite images to measure green space and reports a link rather than a cause, admitting that income or other factors could explain it. It sits mid-scale because a one-off snapshot cannot show what causes what, only summary figures are shared, the journal is not top-tier and the paper is paywalled.

title.note: 'Association' tells readers this is a link, not proof that green space improves mental health; a link is exactly what this kind of study can show.

access.note: The paper sits behind a paywall with no free copy mentioned, so most people cannot read it in full, though price says nothing about quality.

source.note: A legitimate journal where independent experts check studies before publication (peer review), but not one of the most demanding in its field.

theory.note: It builds soundly on established ideas from environmental psychology about nature easing stress, but mainly tests a link those ideas already predict rather than adding a new argument.

methods.note: Survey data from 15,000 adults in 50 cities and greenery measured objectively from satellites are strengths, but a one-off snapshot cannot show cause and only summary figures are shared.

conclusion.note: The authors claim only a link, admit that wealthier, less stressed people may simply move near parks and call for experiments to test cause and effect.

title: The effect of a probiotic yogurt on immune function markers
access: Press release; full study not published.
overview: Tests proprietary bacterial strains. Uses 'immune function' vaguely (the immune system has hundreds of components: which one improved?).
methods: Company internal study. Measured one non-specific immune marker (IgA in saliva) in 30 people for 2 weeks. No control group, no published protocol. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Marketing claims. The press release's claim of an 80% boost refers to a temporary spike in one immune marker, not actual infection resistance or health outcomes.
source: Food Company Press Release. Not peer-reviewed. Study conducted by company employees.

feedback.summary: This is a company press release, not a published study: 30 people, two weeks, one immune marker, no comparison group and no data to check. The '80% boost' is a brief rise in one marker, not a measure of better health. It sits just above the bottom because the question it asks is at least a fair one.

title.note: Sober wording, but 'effect' implies the yogurt caused a change, which a study with no comparison group cannot show; 'markers' also suggests more than the one measured.

access.note: Only a press release is available and the full study has not been published, so nobody can read or check what was actually done.

source.note: A food company's own press release about a study run by its employees, with no independent experts checking it before release.

theory.note: Asking whether a probiotic (food with live bacteria) affects immunity is fair, but 'immune function' is used vaguely for a system with hundreds of parts.

methods.note: Thirty people for two weeks, one general marker (IgA, an antibody in saliva), no comparison group, no published plan and no data: far too little to rely on.

conclusion.note: Calling a short-lived rise in one marker an '80% boost' is a marketing claim: it says nothing about resistance to infection or overall health, neither of which was measured.

title: Psilocybin-assisted therapy for treatment-resistant depression: A double-blind RCT
overview: Investigates psychedelic therapy for depression. Builds on neuroscience of serotonin receptors and psychological theories of set/setting in psychedelic therapy.
methods: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. N=100 patients who failed at least 2 antidepressants. Rigorous screening, therapy protocol standardised, independent assessors. 6-month follow-up. Preregistered. Data availability: Full anonymised data has been deposited in a controlled-access repository; access requires a formal application reviewed by an independent ethics committee, which in practice takes several months and is not straightforward for independent researchers.
conclusion: Careful interpretation. Shows significant symptom reduction but notes therapy protocol was intensive (not just the drug alone), some patients relapsed and long-term safety still unknown. Calls for larger trials.
source: Top-Tier Psychiatry Journal. Known for conservative editorial standards and emphasis on clinical significance.

feedback.summary: A carefully run trial, free to read in a top journal: chance decided who got psilocybin or a dummy treatment, neither patients nor researchers knew which and the plan was published in advance. Its conclusion admits relapses and unknown long-term safety. It misses the top score because 100 patients is modest and the data take months to obtain.

title.note: 'Assisted therapy' rightly signals the drug came with therapy; 'double-blind RCT' names a randomised controlled trial (groups set by chance) where neither patients nor researchers knew who got psilocybin.

access.note: It is open access, so anyone can read the full trial report free of charge and check the results for themselves.

source.note: A top psychiatry journal known for cautious editorial standards and a focus on whether results make a real difference to patients (clinical significance).

theory.note: It builds on brain science about serotonin (a chemical messenger) and on how mindset and surroundings shape the drug experience, to tackle depression that other drugs have not helped.

methods.note: A placebo (dummy treatment) group, independent assessors, a plan published in advance and six-month follow-up make this rigorous, though 100 patients is modest and data access takes months.

conclusion.note: It reports a clear drop in symptoms but notes the benefit came with intensive therapy, not the drug alone, that some patients relapsed and that long-term safety is unknown.

title: A review of the health risks of genetically modified crops by an industry panel
access: Free report on biotech industry association website.
overview: Reviews existing literature on GMO safety. However, panel members are all employed by biotech companies, a clear conflict of interest.
methods: Narrative review (not systematic). Cherry-picks studies showing safety; ignores research raising concerns about pesticide use and biodiversity. No independent critical appraisal. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Biased summary. While many GMOs are likely safe to eat, the panel ignores environmental concerns and dismisses any contrary evidence as 'anti-science'.
source: Industry Association Report. All authors work for GMO-producing companies. Not independent or peer-reviewed.

feedback.summary: This report was written entirely by staff of companies that make genetically modified (GM) crops, with no independent review. It picks studies that show safety, ignores concerns about pesticide use and biodiversity and dismisses opposing evidence as 'anti-science'. Many GM crops may well be safe to eat, but this bias outweighs the report's free access and honest title.

title.note: Plain and accurate: it says this is an industry panel's review of health risks, which helps readers spot a possible conflict of interest.

access.note: The report is free on the industry association's website, but easy access says nothing about whether a review is balanced.

source.note: An industry association report written entirely by staff of companies that make GM crops, so the authors have a stake in the answer; no independent experts checked it.

theory.note: Summarising existing research on GM crop safety adds little that is new; a panel made up only of biotech employees is also unlikely to weigh that research fairly.

methods.note: A narrative review lets authors choose which studies to include, unlike a systematic one that sets search rules in advance; here they left out research raising concerns (cherry-picking).

conclusion.note: Even if many GM crops are likely safe to eat, ignoring environmental concerns and calling all contrary evidence 'anti-science' is one-sided rather than careful.

title: Accelerating sea level rise through 2100: An analysis of global climate models
overview: Uses ensemble of climate models (CMIP6) with updated ice sheet dynamics. Builds on established physics of thermal expansion and glaciology.
methods: Multi-model comparison with rigorous uncertainty quantification. Incorporates satellite data, tide gauges and palaeoclimate proxies for validation. Preregistered methodology. Data availability: All model outputs and code archived in public repositories.
conclusion: Sobering but precise. Projects 0.6–1.1 m rise by 2100 under current emissions trajectory, with clear uncertainty ranges and regional variations. Acknowledges ice sheet behaviour is the largest source of uncertainty.
source: Top-Tier Earth Science Journal. Highest standards for climate model reporting and reproducibility.

feedback.summary: This study does well on every criterion: free to read in a leading journal, built on well-established physics, with a method fixed in advance, checks against real-world records and all model results and code made public. Its conclusion gives a range rather than a single figure and names ice sheets as the biggest unknown. It earns the top score.

title.note: It states the main finding and makes clear it comes from an analysis of climate models, so readers know the results are estimates, not measurements.

access.note: It is open access, so anyone can read the full paper; the model results and code behind it are public too.

source.note: A top earth science journal with the highest standards for reporting climate models and making work reproducible (possible for others to repeat and get the same results).

theory.note: It combines a set of established climate models with updated knowledge of how ice sheets behave, building on well-understood physics such as water expanding as it warms.

methods.note: Comparing many models, measuring uncertainty, checking against satellites, tide gauges and past-climate records, publishing the plan in advance and sharing all results and code make this close to ideal.

conclusion.note: It projects a rise of 0.6 to 1.1 metres by 2100 if emissions stay on their current path, shows regional differences and admits ice sheets are the biggest uncertainty.

title: A laboratory analysis of alleged mind-control chemicals in aircraft contrails ('chemtrails')
access: Anonymous blog post with blurry photos.
overview: Conspiracy theory. Contrails (condensation trails from aircraft) are ice crystals formed from the water vapour in engine exhaust, not chemicals. Basic atmospheric science debunks this.
methods: No credible methodology. Shows photos of normal contrails. Claims to have 'lab analysis' but provides no chain of custody, no lab credentials, no peer review. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Fabricated. No evidence provided. Contradicts fundamental chemistry and meteorology.
source: Anonymous Blog. No credentials, no review, no accountability. Site also promotes New World Order conspiracy theories.

feedback.summary: An anonymous blog post that claims a lab analysis but shows only photos of ordinary contrails, with no lab credentials, no record of how samples were handled and no data. Its mind-control claim contradicts basic science about how contrails form. Free access is its only strength and cannot make up for that, so it gets the lowest rating.

title.note: 'A laboratory analysis' sounds scientific, but the post shows no lab credentials and no data, so the title promises far more than the work behind it delivers.

access.note: Anyone can read the blog post for free, but being easy to reach says nothing about whether its claims are true.

source.note: An anonymous blog with no credentials or review, so nobody is accountable for what it says; the site also promotes New World Order conspiracy theories.

theory.note: Contrails are ice crystals that form from the water vapour in engine exhaust; the post ignores this basic atmospheric science and offers a conspiracy theory instead.

methods.note: Photos of normal contrails and an unverified 'lab analysis', with no chain of custody (a record of who handled the samples) and no data, give nothing anyone could check.

conclusion.note: Its claim of mind-control chemicals rests on no evidence at all and contradicts basic chemistry and meteorology (the science of weather and the atmosphere).

title: Effectiveness of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in reducing HIV transmission risk in a real-world cohort
overview: Follows high-risk individuals taking daily PrEP medication. Grounded in virology and pharmacokinetics of antiretroviral drugs.
methods: Prospective cohort of 5,000 participants. Adherence monitored via pharmacy refills and drug level testing. Compared to matched historical controls. Independent outcome ascertainment. Data availability: De-identified data on request.
conclusion: Strong evidence but emphasises adherence. Near-perfect protection when taken consistently, but effectiveness drops sharply with missed doses. Notes PrEP doesn't protect against other STIs. Notably, the effectiveness estimates rest on comparison to historical controls rather than a concurrent randomised group — a meaningful methodological limitation the authors acknowledge only briefly in the supplementary material.
source: Top-Tier Infectious Disease Journal. Rigorous review and high clinical relevance standards.

feedback.summary: A study of 5,000 people taking PrEP (a daily medicine to prevent HIV), free to read in a top journal. It honestly says missed doses sharply cut protection. It misses the top score because it compares users with people from past records rather than a group set by chance, shares data only on request and mentions that weakness only briefly.

title.note: It names the medicine, the outcome and the setting; 'real-world cohort' (a group followed in everyday life) describes the design without promising any particular result.

access.note: It is open access, so anyone can read the full paper free of charge and check the claims for themselves.

source.note: A top infectious disease journal with strict peer review (checks by independent experts before publication) and high standards for relevance to patient care.

theory.note: PrEP is a daily medicine taken to prevent HIV. The study builds on virology (the science of viruses) and how the body handles the drug, testing it in everyday life.

methods.note: Following 5,000 people and testing drug levels are strengths, but they are compared with past records (historical controls), not a group set by chance; data are shared only on request.

conclusion.note: It is honest that protection drops with missed doses and does not cover other STIs (sexually transmitted infections), but mentions its key weakness only briefly, in the supplementary material.

title: The effect of testosterone therapy on youth and vitality in men over 40
overview: Promotes off-label testosterone use for 'anti-ageing'. Downplays cardiovascular risks and ignores endocrinology showing normal age-related decline isn't a disease.
methods: Retrospective review of clinic patients (no control group). Patients self-selected for treatment and reported 'feeling better' (subjective). No long-term safety monitoring. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Irresponsible. Conflates correlation with causation and ignores possible side effects (blood clots, heart rhythm problems, prostate issues) whose long-term risks are still being studied. Written by clinic owner who profits from selling testosterone.
source: Men's Health Magazine / Clinic Advertising. Not peer-reviewed. Author owns testosterone clinic mentioned in article.

feedback.summary: Written by a clinic owner who sells testosterone and not peer-reviewed, this looks back at clinic patients who chose the treatment and said they felt better. With no comparison group, long-term safety checks or data, it cannot show the hormone caused the improvement. Its use of real patient records, however flawed, lifts it above the lowest rating.

title.note: It avoids words like 'miracle', but 'effect' implies the hormone caused a change and 'youth and vitality' is vague, appealing wording for patients simply saying they felt better.

access.note: It appeared as an article in a supplement industry magazine rather than a research journal, with no data, so even readers who find it have little to check.

source.note: Magazine content and clinic advertising with no peer review (checks by independent experts), written by the owner of the testosterone clinic it mentions, who profits from selling the hormone.

theory.note: It treats the normal drop in testosterone with age as a disease, ignoring endocrinology (the science of hormones) and playing down risks to the heart and blood vessels.

methods.note: Records of clinic patients who chose the treatment and said they felt better, with no comparison group, long-term safety checks or data, cannot separate a real effect from expectation.

conclusion.note: It treats men feeling better as proof the hormone worked (correlation is not causation) and skips over possible side effects such as blood clots, whose long-term risks are still unclear.

title: Correction of the sickle cell mutation in a human patient trial using CRISPR gene editing
overview: Uses CRISPR-Cas9 to edit patient's own haematopoietic stem cells, correcting the genetic mutation causing sickle cell disease. Grounded in molecular biology and gene therapy.
methods: Single-arm trial (no control group; common in early gene-therapy trials, but it makes the benefit harder to judge). N=15 patients with severe sickle cell disease. 2-year follow-up. Rigorous safety monitoring. Data availability: Patient-level data restricted; summary data in paper.
conclusion: The title overclaims for a 15-patient single-arm trial. 'Correction of the mutation' implies completeness that two years of follow-up cannot yet establish. The paper itself is more careful: all patients showed meaningful improvement, but long-term durability is unknown, the procedure is extremely expensive and off-target editing was detected in 2 patients (ongoing monitoring required).
source: Top-Tier Medical Journal. Requires independent data monitoring boards for clinical trials.

feedback.summary: A gene-editing trial for sickle cell disease in a top medical journal, with close safety monitoring and an honest paper that reports unintended edits in two patients. The expert's 6 gives most weight to these strengths; on the rubric alone, the paywall, just 15 patients with no comparison group and an overclaiming title would put it nearer the middle.

title.note: It names the method and makes clear this was a patient trial, but 'correction' suggests a complete, lasting fix that a two-year trial of 15 patients cannot yet show.

access.note: A paywall stops most readers from checking the trial for themselves, although the price of a paper says nothing about whether the research is sound.

source.note: A top medical journal that insists trials are overseen by an independent data monitoring board (outside experts who check safety and results while the trial runs).

theory.note: It builds on molecular biology and gene therapy, using CRISPR (a tool for cutting and editing DNA) on patients' own blood-forming stem cells, aiming to correct the faulty gene.

methods.note: Just 15 patients and no comparison group make the benefit harder to judge and patients' individual data stay private, although close safety monitoring over two years is a strength.

conclusion.note: Unlike the title, the paper is careful: all patients improved, but it admits nobody knows how long this lasts, notes the high cost and reports unintended edits in two patients.

title: The efficacy of an organic diet in preventing all diseases: A 10-year study
access: Published on organic food industry website.
overview: Massively overstates findings. 'All diseases' claim ignores genetics, smoking, exercise and countless other factors.
methods: Observational study comparing organic food shoppers to general population. No control for income, education or overall healthy lifestyle (people who buy organic often exercise more, smoke less, etc.). Data availability: Not provided.
conclusion: Misleading. Any observed health differences likely due to confounding factors (wealthier, health-conscious people) not the organic label itself.
source: Organic Trade Association Report. Study funded by organic industry. Authors work for organic certification bodies.

feedback.summary: A report funded by the organic industry and written by people who work in it, claiming that organic food prevents 'all diseases'. It shares no data and compares organic shoppers with everyone else while ignoring obvious differences such as income and lifestyle. Still, studying real groups of people lifts it just above the lowest rating.

title.note: Claiming that one diet prevents 'all diseases' goes far beyond what any study could show; sweeping headlines like this should put readers on guard.

access.note: It is published on an organic food industry website, so it is easy to reach, but easy access says nothing about whether a report is fair.

source.note: A report from an organic trade association, funded by the industry and written by staff of bodies that certify food as organic, so they have a stake in the result.

theory.note: It credits organic food with preventing every disease, ignoring what is already known about other factors such as genes, smoking and exercise.

methods.note: Organic shoppers are compared with the general population without taking account of income, education or healthy habits, any of which could explain a difference; no data are shared either.

conclusion.note: It treats a link as proof, but organic buyers tend to be wealthier and more health-conscious (confounding factors), so any health difference likely comes from these, not the organic label.

title: The effect of hourly breaks from sitting on metabolic risk markers in office workers
overview: Tests interrupting prolonged sitting with short activity breaks. Based on metabolic physiology and epidemiology of sedentary behaviour.
methods: Randomised crossover trial. N=40 participants. Measured blood glucose, insulin and lipids after 8-hour sitting vs sitting interrupted by 3-minute walks every hour. Lab-controlled conditions. Preregistered. Data availability: Full data on OSF.
conclusion: Measured findings. Shows improvements in glucose metabolism but notes this was short-term, in controlled conditions. Doesn't claim breaks alone prevent diabetes or heart disease.
source: Respected Exercise Physiology Journal. Good methodological standards.

feedback.summary: Strong on every criterion: open access, a respected journal, a randomised design with a plan fixed in advance and all data shared, plus a conclusion that claims no more than it found. The expert's 5 seems to weigh its limits heavily: short-term lab tests on 40 people cannot show lasting benefits in real offices.

title.note: It names what was tested and what was measured, 'metabolic risk markers' (blood readings linked to later illness), rather than claiming breaks prevent diabetes or heart disease.

access.note: It is open access and the full data are public too, so anyone can read the paper and check the results for themselves.

source.note: A respected journal of exercise physiology (how the body responds to activity), with good standards for how research is designed and carried out.

theory.note: It builds on population studies of sitting and health (epidemiology) and on how the body handles sugar and fat, then tests the idea directly with an experiment.

methods.note: A randomised crossover trial (each person tries both conditions in random order), preregistered and with full data public; its main weakness is a small sample of 40.

conclusion.note: It reports better blood sugar handling but notes the test was short and lab-based; it does not claim breaks alone prevent diabetes or heart disease.

title: The efficacy of a 'detox' tea for toxin removal and adipose tissue reduction
access: Influencer Instagram post with affiliate link.
overview: Scientifically nonsensical. The liver and kidneys detoxify the body; no tea can 'flush toxins', as the post claims, and fat cannot be spot-reduced from the belly.
methods: No study. Influencer's personal testimonial plus paid actors in before/after photos. No measurements, no controls, no biology. Data availability: None.
conclusion: Fraudulent marketing. The tea is a laxative causing temporary water weight loss (and dehydration), not fat loss.
source: Social Media Influencer. Paid promotion. No scientific credentials. Breaks advertising rules by not labelling the post as an advert.

feedback.summary: There is no study, only an influencer paid to promote the tea, paid actors in before-and-after photos and no label saying it is an advert. Its claims contradict basic biology and the tea is a laxative, so any weight lost is water that soon returns. Easy access is its only strength and says nothing about whether the claims are true.

title.note: Research words like 'efficacy' (how well something works) and 'adipose tissue' (body fat) dress an advert up as science; the title also assumes a tea can remove toxins.

access.note: Anyone can see an Instagram post, but easy access is not the same as trustworthiness: the affiliate link pays the influencer for every sale it brings in.

source.note: A paid promotion by an influencer with no scientific qualifications, which breaks advertising rules by not saying it is an advert; the person making the claims profits from them.

theory.note: It ignores basic biology: the liver and kidneys already clear toxins from the body and fat cannot be lost from one chosen spot such as the belly.

methods.note: There is no study at all, just the influencer's own story and before-and-after photos of paid actors, with nothing measured, nothing compared and no data.

conclusion.note: Its promise of toxin removal and fat loss is false: as a laxative (it speeds up the bowels), the tea only causes a brief loss of water weight, risking dehydration.

title: The impact of participatory budgeting on civic engagement in marginalised communities
overview: Studies democratic innovation where residents directly decide local spending. Grounded in political science theories of deliberative democracy and empowerment.
methods: Mixed methods: quantitative analysis of voting records across 30 cities plus qualitative interviews with participants. Preregistered analysis. Control cities matched on demographics. Data availability: Quantitative data public; interview transcripts available on request (privacy).
conclusion: Nuanced. Shows increased participation in marginalised groups but notes effects vary by implementation quality and existing political culture. Doesn't claim participatory budgeting solves all governance problems.
source: Top-Tier Political Science Journal. Known for rigorous mixed-methods standards.

feedback.summary: This study does well on every criterion: free to read in a top journal, with an analysis plan fixed in advance, matched comparison cities, interviews and public voting data. Its conclusion admits results depend on how well the scheme is run. That earns the top score, although cities were not assigned to the scheme at random, so some doubt remains.

title.note: Plain and specific: it names the policy, the outcome (civic engagement: taking part in public life) and the communities studied, without promising any particular result.

access.note: It is open access and the voting data are public, so anyone can read the paper and check the numbers for themselves.

source.note: A top political science journal known for strict standards in mixed-methods research, which combines numbers with interviews.

theory.note: It builds on political science theories of deliberative democracy (citizens discussing and deciding together) to test participatory budgeting, where residents decide directly how local money is spent.

methods.note: Voting records from 30 cities (made public), interviews and an analysis plan fixed in advance (preregistration) are strengths; comparison cities matched on population make-up may still differ in other ways.

conclusion.note: It reports more participation by marginalised groups but admits results depend on how well the scheme is run and on local political culture, without claiming it fixes everything.

title: The efficacy of magnets in curing arthritis pain by realigning 'body energy fields'
access: Free PDF on magnet therapy sales website.
overview: Pseudoscience. The human body has no 'energy fields' that magnets could affect. Magnetic fields do pass through the body (MRI scanners rely on this), but a small therapy magnet's field weakens rapidly with distance and there is no known way it could relieve pain.
methods: No controlled study. Testimonials from customers who bought magnetic bracelets. No comparison to placebo (which is powerful for subjective pain). Data availability: None.
conclusion: Placebo effect being sold as medicine. Systematic reviews of actual controlled trials show magnetic therapy performs no better than fake magnets.
source: Magnet Therapy Company Website. Selling magnets for £150 each. Site also claims magnets cure diabetes and cancer.

feedback.summary: A sales document from a company that charges £150 per magnet and claims magnets cure diabetes and cancer. It rests on 'body energy fields' that do not exist and on customer stories with no comparison against fake magnets, while reviews of fair tests find magnets work no better than fakes. Being a free download is its only strength.

title.note: The promise of 'curing' pain is a red flag and the title takes for granted 'body energy fields', which do not exist.

access.note: The PDF is free to download, but it sits on a website selling magnets; easy access says nothing about whether a claim is true.

source.note: The company behind it sells the magnets at £150 each and also claims they cure diabetes and cancer, so it has every reason to exaggerate.

theory.note: It relies on 'energy fields' the body does not have; magnetic fields do pass through us, as hospital MRI scanners show, but a small magnet's field fades quickly with distance.

methods.note: Only stories from customers who bought bracelets, with no comparison against fake magnets, which matters because pain is especially open to the placebo effect (feeling better because you expect to).

conclusion.note: It sells a placebo effect as medicine; systematic reviews (studies that pool the results of many fair tests) find magnets work no better than fake ones.
